intro: Rotterdam's old trees are survivors first and monuments second. The German bombing of May 1940 erased most of the city centre in a single night, and the soft, subsiding soil across much of the region shortens most trees' working lives regardless of what happens above ground; the city has barely 3,000 monumental trees against 600,000 total. What remains earned its place the hard way: a plane that predates the park built around it, another that survived the exact firestorm that flattened everything nearby, a coronation linden, a beech that watched the shipping elite build their street.
meta_description: Rotterdam's oldest trees survived what the city itself often didn't: the 1940 bombing, the 1953 flood, a canal redesign. 17 verified locations.
question_answer: Rotterdam's oldest tree is the Plane of het Park, standing since around 1800, before landscape architects Jan David and Louis Paul Zocher designed the park around it in 1852. At roughly 226 years old, it has survived both the 1940 bombing that destroyed much of the city centre and the 1953 flood that put het Park itself underwater.
question_meta: A plane tree older than the park around it, standing since 1800, survived the 1940 bombing and the 1953 flood. Rotterdam's oldest, plus sixteen more.
question_context: Rotterdam's tree ages tell a story most Dutch cities don't have to tell: almost everything old here either predates the 20th century's two great disasters or was planted afterward to replace what didn't survive them. The Park Plane and the Breitenbach Plane both cleared the German bombing of 14 May 1940 that flattened the historic centre a short walk from each of them, and the Park Plane cleared a second disaster besides, the 1953 flood that put much of the park underwater for weeks. That double survival is the actual basis for calling it Rotterdam's oldest confirmed tree rather than simply its most storied one; several other candidates are old enough to be plausible rivals but lack a comparably documented history reaching back before 1900. The Wilhelmina Linden and the Koningin Emmaplein Beech are both younger by a wide enough margin, planted within a few decades of each other in the 1890s, that the ranking among Rotterdam's oldest three genuinely rests on the two 19th-century-or-earlier planes rather than any of the turn-of-the-century additions.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Rotterdam?
faq.a: The Plane of het Park, standing since around 1800, older than the park itself, which was designed around it starting in 1852.

faq.q: Are Rotterdam's remarkable trees free to visit?
faq.a: Most stand in public parks or on public streets, open at any time, no ticket required. Three, the beech and two cedars in the Historic Garden of Schoonoord, need entering a gated garden that is free but keeps daily opening hours. Four more, in Arboretum Trompenburg, a separate botanical garden about 3km from the rest, need a paid ticket.

faq.q: Why does Rotterdam have so few monumental trees?
faq.a: The German bombing of 14 May 1940 destroyed most of the historic centre in a single night, and much of the region's soft, subsiding soil shortens trees' working lives regardless of what happens above ground.

faq.q: Which Rotterdam tree is named after a poet?
faq.a: The Breitenbach Plane on the Westersingel, named for South African poet Breyten Breytenbach, who recited poetry beneath it in the 1970s and called it the grave of the unknown poet.

trees.name: The Park Plane

location.address: het Park, near the Euromast, Rotterdam Centrum

trees.story: This plane tree was already standing when father-and-son landscape architects Jan David and Louis Paul Zocher began designing het Park around it in 1852, which means the tree came first and the celebrated English-style landscape grew up around a specimen nobody planted specifically for the design. It has since survived two disasters that reshaped Rotterdam far more than any garden ever could. The German bombing of May 1940 destroyed most of the city's historic centre a short walk away; the tree stood close enough to feel it and far enough to survive. Thirteen years later the North Sea flood of 1953 put het Park itself underwater for an extended stretch, one of the worst natural disasters in modern Dutch history, and the tree came through that too, roots submerged in salt water that killed less established trees outright. Today its trunk measures 185 centimetres across, thick enough that the city's own tree inspectors check it on a regular safety schedule reserved for its most significant specimens. Het Park itself is a national monument, 21 hectares running along the Maas river beside the Euromast, and this plane is the one tree in it old enough to have watched the whole modern city rebuild itself twice.
trees.access: Free, open park at any time
trees.transport: Walkable from central Rotterdam, near the Euromast, roughly 15 minutes
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its age: this is the tree het Park was laid out around from 1852, the only one there older than the park itself. It stands in het Park, near the Euromast, on the safety schedule the city keeps for its biggest trees.
trees.verify_notes: 2026-09-08: the story says the trunk 'measures 185 centimetres across', and that is ambiguous in a way that changes the tree. Across reads as diameter in English, which would make it 5.81 metres round; Dutch registers publish omtrek, girth, and 185 cm of girth would be an ordinary tree rather than one het Park was designed around in 1852. The national register carries no entry within 120 metres of our pin, so it cannot settle it here. girth_cm is deliberately left empty rather than filled with either reading, and the recognition line does not use the number.

trees.name: The Breitenbach Plane
trees.story: This plane tree has been standing since 1860, older than the Westersingel canal that now runs beside it, and it survived the one event that erased almost everything else nearby: the German bombing of Rotterdam's city centre on 14 May 1940, which burned through this exact stretch of the city and somehow left the tree unscathed. Decades of care since have earned it an unofficial title, the most expensive tree in Rotterdam, for the sustained municipal maintenance a tree this old and this large now requires. It nearly lost a different fight in the 1960s, when a major redesign of the Westersingel waterway put the tree directly in the way of new plans; the city's own head of landscaping at the time, Andre Raad, pushed back hard enough that engineers rerouted the water instead of felling the tree, an unusual case of a canal moving to accommodate a plant rather than the other way round. Its more recent name comes from South African poet Breyten Breytenbach, who recited poetry beneath it in the 1970s and declared it the grave of the unknown poet, a line that stuck well enough that Rotterdam's own Poetry International later gave the spot a permanent place in the city's poetry trail. It still stands at the corner of Mauritsweg and Westersingel, doing the same job it has done since before the Netherlands had a railway.
trees.access: Free, public street at any time
trees.transport: Walkable from central Rotterdam, roughly 10 minutes
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its place on Rotterdam's poetry trail, the spot where Breyten Breytenbach recited and called it the grave of the unknown poet. It stands on the corner of Mauritsweg and Westersingel.

official_register.name: Landelijk Register van Monumentale Bomen (Bomenstichting), no. 1684847

trees.name: The Wilhelmina Linden
trees.story: An 18-year-old queen's coronation once triggered a small nationwide planting spree, and this linden on the Parklaan is Rotterdam's surviving entry in it. When Wilhelmina was crowned Queen of the Netherlands on 6 September 1898, a metalworks foundry in Doetinchem sent a brochure to every Dutch municipality suggesting they mark the occasion with a commemorative tree, offering to supply the decorative iron fencing to go around it. Towns across the country took up the idea, and Rotterdam planted this Crimean linden on the Parklaan, in what was then a fashionable new residential quarter for the city's shipping merchants. The tree's iron fence has outlasted plenty of the era's other civic gestures: it holds its own listing on the Dutch national heritage register, a decorative object protected separately from the tree it surrounds, which is either a bureaucratic curiosity or a sign of how seriously the country still takes its handful of surviving coronation trees. At roughly 128 years old, the linden has outlived the queen it honours by more than seven decades and stands a quiet, well-tended reminder that Rotterdam's grandest 19th-century street was, for one afternoon in 1898, briefly about a young monarch rather than shipping money.

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the decorative iron fence around it, which holds its own listing on the Dutch national heritage register. It stands on the Parklaan in the Scheepvaartkwartier, planted for Wilhelmina's coronation in 1898.

trees.name: The Koningin Emmaplein Beech
trees.story: Fifteen grand townhouses built between 1888 and 1891 once earned this small square a joking nickname, Rijkeluishofje, the rich people's almshouse, a dig at how sheltered and comfortable its wealthy residents had it compared with the actual almshouses the word usually described. The copper beech at its centre went into the ground around the same years the houses went up, planted alongside a decorative 1890 urn designed by Hendrik Berlage, the architect who would later define much of Amsterdam's own cityscape. The neo-renaissance townhouses around the square housed Rotterdam's shipping elite, close enough to the harbour to manage their businesses and far enough from it to avoid the noise and smell, and the beech has stood at the centre of that arrangement for roughly 135 years, its trunk now 325 centimetres around. Copper beeches are planted for their colour, deep purple-red leaves that shift with the season and light rather than staying a uniform green, and this one has had over a century to fill out into the kind of specimen that makes an otherwise ordinary residential square worth a detour. It remains free and open, a short walk from the Westersingel and Parklaan trees on the same side of the city centre.
verified_sources: https://www.rotterdam.nl/monumentale-bomen (LRMB record nr 1695436, Bruine beuk Koningin Emmaplein, single-tree point; red beech planted when the square was built, 1888-1891)

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the purple-red leaves and the trunk, 325 centimetres around. It stands at the centre of Koningin Emmaplein, beside the 1890 urn designed by Hendrik Berlage, with the square's fifteen townhouses around it.

trees.name: The Lijnbaan Plane

location.address: Small square on the southern end of the Lijnbaan, Rotterdam

trees.story:
This plane was likely planted in 1851 in the garden of the Coolsingel hospital, and it was still there in May 1940 when German bombing destroyed most of Rotterdam's city centre in a single night, the hospital included. Only the tree and the building's entrance gate came through. The gate stands beside the plane today, the two of them forming what Rotterdammers now treat as an accidental monument neither was designed to be.

The tree nearly lost a different fight two decades later. When the Lijnbaan, one of Europe's first purpose-built pedestrian shopping streets, was extended and renovated in the 1960s, the plan called for a dead straight line the tree and gate stood directly in the way of. Shopkeepers fought the compromise that saved them and lost; the street bent anyway, a small square was built around the tree instead, and the shops went up around that. A Rotterdam poet, Pascale Duin, later wrote it an ode calling it a silent witness. In 2019 it was nominated to represent the whole province of Zuid-Holland in the national Tree of the Year contest. It stands free, in the open, one of two Rotterdam planes known to have survived the exact night that erased almost everything around them.
trees.access: Free, public square, open at any time
trees.transport: Centrum, central Rotterdam; about a 10 minute walk from Rotterdam Centraal station
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by standing beside the lone surviving hospital gate, in a small square the street bends around instead of running straight. It stands at the southern end of the Lijnbaan.

trees.name: The Memorial Yew of Eendrachtsplein
trees.story:
Rotterdam spent its first postwar years rebuilding rather than remembering, and it took one person to insist on a place to do both: Willem Ganter, first violinist of the Rotterdam Philharmonic Orchestra, who raised money for a memorial tree at the garden of the police station on Eendrachtsplein, a spot the city had trusted people to gather at even during the occupation. A 20-year-old European yew was ordered from England and planted in 1947, already a substantial tree rather than a sapling, because a memorial planted small would have taken decades to look like one.

The yew has had a harder life since than the plan intended. A new tram line cut through the area, then a metro line in 1983, and the police eventually moved out of the building entirely, which is now a cafe. The tree itself once grew on two trunks and now stands on one, having lost the other somewhere along the way, and simply outlasted every change around it regardless. Had Ganter chosen a less tenacious species, none of this would have survived to be told. It stands free, in the open, beside the entrance of the building it has outlived every use of.
trees.access: Free, public street, viewable at any time
trees.transport: Centrum, central Rotterdam; about a 12 minute walk from Rotterdam Centraal station

best_time.label: September to November: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its single trunk, having lost a second it once had, beside the entrance of the former police station, now a cafe. It stands at Eendrachtsplein 3.

trees.name: The Planes of Delftseplein
trees.species: London Plane and Oriental Plane (Platanus x acerifolia and Platanus orientalis)

location.address: Delftseplein, just east of Rotterdam Centraal station, Rotterdam

trees.story:
Four planes, three London and one Oriental, went into the ground together around 1860 as planting around a pond that once sat in front of Rotterdam's original Centraal Station entrance. The pond and that entrance are both gone, replaced by later station buildings, but the trees stayed on Delftseplein through every rebuild the station itself went through, including the one that flattened most of the surrounding neighbourhood in May 1940.

Mixing Oriental plane in with the more common London plane hybrid in one planting was not unusual for 19th-century Dutch civic gardening, a hedge against uncertainty about which would thrive better on reclaimed, disturbed ground next to a working rail yard. Whichever species won that test is no longer the point; all four have made it past a century and a half. They stand together, free, immediately east of the current station building, close enough that anyone stepping off a train into Rotterdam is likely to walk past the oldest trees on the whole route without knowing it.
trees.access: Free, public square, open at any time
trees.transport: Immediately east of Rotterdam Centraal station
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by the group of four planes standing together, three London and one Oriental. They stand on Delftseplein, just east of Rotterdam Centraal.

trees.name: The Plane of Westersingel

location.address: Westersingel at the crossing with Mauritsweg and Witte de Withstraat, Rotterdam

trees.story:
This London plane stands at a junction most people pass through rather than stop at, where the Westersingel canal crosses the Mauritsweg and Witte de Withstraat, planted sometime around 1900 to 1910 as the streets around it took their current shape. It is younger than the two more storied planes elsewhere on the same Westersingel, the one that survived the 1940 bombing and the one a South African poet once read verse beneath, and it carries no comparable story of its own beyond simply having grown steadily at a crossing for over a century.

That plainness is not nothing. Most street trees this old in a heavily bombed, heavily rebuilt city do not make it, and this one has, standing through whatever traffic patterns and canal-side redevelopment the junction has seen since the Edwardian era. It grows in the open, free, on the same short stretch of canal that carries two of Rotterdam's more famous trees, worth a stop on the same walk rather than a destination by itself.
trees.access: Free, public street, open at any time
trees.transport: Centrum, central Rotterdam; about a 12 minute walk from Rotterdam Centraal station
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by standing at the junction where the canal crosses Mauritsweg and Witte de Withstraat, plainer than its two famous neighbours nearby. It stands on Westersingel.

trees.name: The Copper Beech of Schoonoord
trees.story:
Schoonoord holds roughly a thousand species of plants and trees inside a garden barely bigger than a football pitch, and this copper beech is one of only two survivors from the day its original layout went in, sometime between 1860 and 1870. Wikipedia separately mentions a '200-year-old beech' among the park's notable trees, but that figure predates the garden itself by decades, so it more likely rounds a different tree or repeats an unverified figure than describes this one. The register's own planting band puts this beech at roughly 155 to 165 years, a more specific and better-sourced number, so that is the one used here, flagged for the conflict rather than resolved by guessing.

The register calls the trunk '125 cm dik', the Dutch word for thickness rather than circumference, which most likely means a diameter near that figure and a girth closer to 390 cm, though the record does not say so directly and it has not been measured independently. Twenty metres tall, crown eighteen metres across, standing beside the garden's pond on a narrow footpath near the Westzeedijk boundary.

Schoonoord is a former country estate, a protected Rijksmonument since 2000, owned by the Stichting Schoonoord and open to the public since 1973 after decades as a private garden. Bees, koi and a resident tawny owl share the grounds. Two ancient Lebanon cedars from the same original planting stand nearby.
trees.access: Free, daily 8:30-16:30 (closes during large festivals in adjoining Het Park)
trees.transport: Walkable from central Rotterdam, near the Euromast, roughly 15 minutes
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by standing beside the garden's pond on a narrow footpath near the Westzeedijk boundary, with two Lebanon cedars nearby. It stands in the Historische Tuin Schoonoord.

trees.name: The Lebanon Cedars of Schoonoord
trees.age_estimate: roughly 155-165 years (register); local sources say over 250 years
trees.story:
Rotterdam's own garden site and Wikipedia both single out this pair as the best-known trees in the whole of Schoonoord, and neither source agrees on how old they are. Standing together at one point in the garden, they read as one feature rather than two.

The estate's own history puts their planting at the garden's original 1860s layout, which would make them roughly 155 to 165 years old today. Wikipedia and several tourism write-ups instead call them 'ruim 250 jaar oud', over 250 years, which would put their planting before the garden existed at all: either they arrived here as already-mature transplants, or the figure is a repeated claim nobody has checked. Neither can be preferred with confidence, so both are recorded rather than one picked over the other.

What is not in dispute is the setting. Schoonoord is a 1.2-hectare former country estate on the Kievitslaan, a protected Rijksmonument since 2000, owned by the Stichting Schoonoord and open to the public since 1973. A copper beech from the same original planting stands nearby. Entry is free, daily from 8:30 to 16:30, though the garden closes during the large festivals held next door in Het Park.
trees.access: Free, daily 8:30-16:30 (closes during large festivals in adjoining Het Park)
trees.transport: Walkable from central Rotterdam, near the Euromast, roughly 15 minutes
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by the pair standing together at one point in the garden, reading as one feature rather than two. They stand in the Historische Tuin Schoonoord.

best_time.label: September to November: upright barrel cones that sit on the branches like eggs

trees.name: The Atlas Cedar of Heemraadspark

location.address: Heemraadssingel, near the Schietbaanbrug, west side near no. 215B, Rotterdam

trees.story:
Rotterdam's own list of monumental trees calls this Atlas cedar '100+ years old', which would put its planting before 1926. The register that catalogued it individually gives an exact year instead, 1930, within a band of 1930 to 1940, which is both more specific and the number used here, flagged against the city's rounder claim.

It stands on municipal land beside the Heemraadssingel canal, near the Schietbaanbrug, a wooden footbridge from 1867 that is itself a listed monument, on the canal's west side near house number 215B. The Heemraadssingel is one of Rotterdam's oldest and best-preserved canals, laid out between roughly 1900 and 1915 as part of a protected cityscape, and today carries about fifty tree species along its banks, mostly planes and lindens. A cedar standing out among them is rare enough to have earned this one its own register entry.

Other sources describe a pair of Atlas cedars further along the same canal, near house number 180, which may or may not be the same trees under a different address; this entry covers the specimen at the register's own coordinate, by the footbridge. The canal and its trees are public at all times, no ticket, no gate, just a path along the water.
trees.access: Free, public canalside park (Heemraadssingel/Heemraadspark), open at any time
trees.transport: Walkable from central Rotterdam, Nieuwe Westen district, roughly 20-25 minutes; also reachable by tram along the singel
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by standing out as a conifer among the canal's planes and lindens, beside the wooden Schietbaanbrug footbridge. It stands on the Heemraadssingel, near number 215B.

trees.name: The Holm Oak of Trompenburg
trees.access: Paid entry to Trompenburg Tuinen & Arboretum (adult ticket; free with the Dutch Museumkaart). Open Tue-Sun 10:00-16:30 and Mon from 12:00 (April onward), shorter hours Nov-Feb.
trees.transport: Tram 21 to Woudestein, then about 5 minutes on foot to the garden entrance at Honingerdijk 86.
trees.story:
In 1928 Trompenburg lost roughly 400 elms to Dutch elm disease, and out of that clearing grew one of the best oak collections in Europe. This holm oak was already here when the saws came. The national register puts its planting between 1910 and 1920, which makes it about 110 years old and older than the arboretum it now stands in.

It is also the odd one out. A holm oak belongs to the Mediterranean, keeps its dark leathery leaves all winter, and looks nothing like the deciduous oaks the garden is famous for. Trompenburg holds the Dutch National Plant Collection of Quercus, and named oaks such as 'Pondaim' and the 'East Column' and 'West Column' forms of Quercus x rosacea were raised here. This evergreen came before all of that.

The garden itself is older still. James Smith laid it out from 1820 on the Honingerdijk, the Zochers, father and son, reworked the western half around 1870, and James van Hoey Smith turned it into an arboretum after the elms fell. His son Dick built the collection up, and the gates opened to the public in 1958.

One honest caveat: the register dates this tree, but the garden's own history does not single it out, and no second source we found names this individual oak. If you know more about it, tell us. It is a separate stop from Rotterdam's other trees, about three kilometres away, with its own ticket.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its leaves: dark, leathery and still on the tree in winter, when most of the collection's oaks stand bare. It stands in section M of the arboretum, accession number 17.

trees.name: The Weeping Pear of Trompenburg
trees.access: Paid entry to Trompenburg Tuinen & Arboretum (adult ticket; free with the Dutch Museumkaart). Open Tue-Sun 10:00-16:30 and Mon from 12:00 (April onward), shorter hours Nov-Feb.
trees.transport: Tram 21 to Woudestein, then about 5 minutes on foot to the garden entrance at Honingerdijk 86.
trees.story:
Of the trees the national register dates inside Arboretum Trompenburg, the oldest is not an oak or a cedar but an ornamental pear. It puts the planting between 1870 and 1880, which makes it roughly 150 years old, half a century older than the arboretum that grew up around it.

Pyrus salicifolia, the willow-leaved pear, is grown for its narrow silver-grey leaves, usually as a small decorative tree rather than a monument. The register calls it a treurpeer, a weeping pear, but names no cultivar, so the familiar drooping 'Pendula' form is likely rather than recorded.

When it went in, Trompenburg was still a private estate on the Honingerdijk: James Smith had laid it out from 1820 and combined it with the neighbouring land in 1859, and the landscape architects Jan David and Louis Paul Zocher reworked the western section around 1870. No source ties this pear to their redesign, so treat that as the setting rather than its origin. It then saw roughly 400 elms felled to Dutch elm disease in 1928, James van Hoey Smith turn the grounds into an arboretum, and the public let in for the first time in 1958.

The register dates it and the garden's history covers the estate, but no second source names this individual tree. If you know its story, tell us. It is a separate stop from Rotterdam's other trees, with its own entry fee.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its narrow, willow-like silver-grey leaves, the mark of the willow-leaved pear. It stands in section C of the arboretum.

trees.name: The Himalayan Cedar of Trompenburg
trees.access: Paid entry to Trompenburg Tuinen & Arboretum (adult ticket; free with the Dutch Museumkaart). Open Tue-Sun 10:00-16:30 and Mon from 12:00 (April onward), shorter hours Nov-Feb.
trees.transport: Tram 21 to Woudestein, then about 5 minutes on foot to the garden entrance at Honingerdijk 86.
trees.story:
You cannot see this cedar from the street. The national register says so outright: it stands inside Arboretum Trompenburg where no passer-by can see it, so the only way to meet it is to buy a ticket and walk in.

The register puts its planting between 1920 and 1930, which makes it roughly a century old. That decade was the garden's turning point. In 1928 roughly 400 elms here were felled to Dutch elm disease, and James van Hoey Smith began turning the estate into a true arboretum. Whether this cedar was part of that first replanting, nothing we found says.

A deodar is a tree of the western Himalaya, with soft blue-green needles and branch tips that droop as if tired. Here it grew up alongside a collection that Dick van Hoey Smith later built into one of international standing. The garden opened to the public in 1958 and received the International Dendrology Society's Conservation Plaquette in 1983.

The register dates it, but no second source names this particular cedar, and we found no published girth or height. If you have measured it, tell us. It is a separate stop from Rotterdam's other old trees, about three kilometres away, with its own entry fee.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the soft blue-green needles and the drooping tips of its leading shoot and branches, the mark of a deodar. It stands in section G of the arboretum.

photo.note: Two similar slim multi-stemmed cedars side by side in Trompenburg (geotag about 60 m, no accuracy), genus-only ID; which one is the section G deodar is not settled and neither trunk clearly reads as 3

trees.name: The Summer Lime of Trompenburg
trees.access: Paid entry to Trompenburg Tuinen & Arboretum (adult ticket; free with the Dutch Museumkaart). Open Tue-Sun 10:00-16:30 and Mon from 12:00 (April onward), shorter hours Nov-Feb.
trees.transport: Tram 21 to Woudestein, then about 5 minutes on foot to the garden entrance at Honingerdijk 86.
trees.story:
Every tree the national register lists inside Arboretum Trompenburg comes with a plot number, except this one. The weeping pear is in section C, the cedar in G, the evergreen oak in M. The large-leaved lime has only the garden's name, which makes it the hardest of them to find by the garden plan.

The register puts its planting between 1930 and 1940, roughly 90 years ago. That places it after 1928, the year roughly 400 elms here fell to Dutch elm disease and James van Hoey Smith began turning the old estate into a real arboretum, so it grew up with the collection rather than before it. Nothing we found says who planted it or why.

It is a native European lime, the large-leaved species, with broader, softer leaves than the common lime lining Dutch streets, downy on the underside. Around it the garden kept growing: Dick van Hoey Smith built the collection into one of international standing, the gates opened to the public in 1958, and the International Dendrology Society awarded the garden its Conservation Plaquette in 1983. Today Trompenburg holds the Dutch National Plant Collections of oak, beech, rhododendron and hosta.

The register dates this tree, but no second source names it individually, and we found no published girth or height. If you have stood under it with a tape measure, tell us. It is a separate stop from Rotterdam's other old trees, about three kilometres away, with its own entry fee.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its broad, soft leaves, downy on the underside, which mark it as a large-leaved lime. It stands roughly 100 metres north of the weeping pear in section C.

best_time.label: scented lime flowers, loud with bees

trees.name: The Wilhelmina Chestnut of Noordereiland

location.address: Burgemeester Hoffmanplein, corner of Van der Takstraat, Noordereiland, Rotterdam

trees.access: Free, open public square (Burgemeester Hoffmanplein) on Noordereiland; no hours.

location_site.name: Burgemeester Hoffmanplein (small square with the Wilhelmina fountain)

trees.verify_notes: Alive per noordereiland.org, 26 June 2026 (updated 30 Sept 2026): the chestnut stands but is in poor health (chestnut bleeding canker plus two life-threatening fungi on the trunk); a large main branch broke off some years ago and was saved by tree surgeons; expected to become a safety risk and be removed 'in a few years'. Not yet removed. Girth 'almost 4 m', height 18-24 m (noordereiland.org, citing tree knight Pim Janse; same figures on the 2022 page). Age disputed: register planted_band 1880-1890 and register history 'planted 1898 for Wilhelmina's accession'; noordereiland.org 2026 says planted 1889 for the inauguration; noordereiland.org 2022 says 'from 1870'; nl.wikipedia says probably planted 1898 with the fountain. Wilhelmina was inaugurated in 1898, so 1889 reads as a typo. Derived age is broad, from the register band plus the 1898 claim; not sharpened. WWII story (register and noordereiland.org agree): known to resistance people as the 'dubbele paardenkastanje' (double chestnut), a Wilhelmina tree residents guarded as a quiet act of resistance; a second story told that it grew on ground where the dead were buried so better not cut; elders in the 1970s said 'come back when it flowers, then you see two flowers'; survived the fighting around Noordereiland and the Maas bridges and the Hunger Winter when trees were felled for fuel; a tale says someone tried to fell it and gave up after one branch. Its roots cracked the Wilhelmina fountain (Evers design, 1898) in the early 1990s; fountain removed, restored and replaced a century after the inauguration (nl.wikipedia). Flowers April-May (noordereiland.org). A second chestnut on the same square opposite the Lelieblok, planted 1920, girth almost 3 m, height 15-18 m, good health, is the SMALLER one; the subject is the larger one at the corner of Van der Takstraat beside the fountain. Pin: register coordinate (nr 1691895, n_trees 1), not checked on aerial imagery; OSM natural=tree nodes on the square carry no species, so approximate. Covered-country rule (NL): no photo and no confirmed pin, so strictly a lead; delivered as flagged for the orchestrator's gate. Commons geosearch within 100 m found no tree photo; lifecheck NONE.
trees.story:
Noordereiland kept this chestnut alive through the Second World War with a ghost story. It was a Wilhelmina tree, and while trees across occupied Rotterdam went for firewood, a tale went round that it grew on ground where the dead lay, and that whoever cut it would bring bad luck on himself and his neighbours. Among resistance people it was known as the double chestnut. In the 1970s older islanders still said it: come back when it flowers, and you will see two flowers.

It came through the fighting around the island and the Maas bridges, and the Hunger Winter. One tale says somebody did try to fell it and gave up after a single branch.

When it went in is less settled. The national register gives 1880 to 1890 and also 1898, for Wilhelmina's accession; Dutch Wikipedia says probably 1898, with the fountain beside it; the island's website has said 1870 and, elsewhere, 1889. That leaves it somewhere between about 125 and 155 years old.

It is almost four metres round and 18 to 24 metres tall. In the early 1990s its roots cracked the Wilhelmina fountain, which was removed, restored and put back.

The news now is not good. The trunk carries bleeding canker and two life-threatening fungi, and a main branch broke off some years ago. Local reporting in 2026 expects it to be felled within a few years. If you want to see the double chestnut in flower, do not wait long.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the larger of the two horse chestnuts on the Burgemeester Hoffmanplein, almost four metres round. It stands at the corner of Van der Takstraat beside the fountain; the smaller one faces the Lelieblok.

best_time.label: late April into May, when white flower candles stand over the whole crown

trees.name: The Copper Beech of Overschie

location.address: Overschiese Dorpsstraat, opposite no. 100, at the Grote Kerk (no. 95), Overschie, Rotterdam

trees.access: Free to view from the street: the register says it stands about six metres from the Overschiese Dorpsstraat, opposite no. 100, and is easy to see from the public road. The ground belongs to the church.
trees.transport: Overschie is in north-west Rotterdam; public transport to the Overschiese Dorpsstraat not checked.
trees.story:
In 1899 lightning burned down Overschie's medieval church. A new Grote Kerk went up, and in 1901, once it was finished, a gardener named Voorhorst planted a copper beech on the church's ground. This is that beech.

The national register of monumental trees, which tells the story, also does the arithmetic. The young tree was probably five to seven years old when Voorhorst put it in, which makes it about 130 years old now. A planting year, an occasion and a gardener's name, all on one tree.

There were once two. The register says a second copper beech was lost to a strong westerly wind; this one is the survivor.

You do not need to go through a gate to see it. The register puts it about six metres back from the Overschiese Dorpsstraat, opposite number 100, and says it is easy to see from the public road. Copper beeches open their leaves purple in spring and turn copper before they fall, so the same tree reads differently in April and in October.

One caveat, stated plainly. The most recent photograph we could find dates from 2021, and a register cannot say whether a tree still stands. If you pass the church, tell us it is there, and if you have a tape measure, how far round it has grown in 130 years.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its purple-brown leaves, the copper beech's colour. It stands about six metres back from the Overschiese Dorpsstraat, opposite number 100, at the Grote Kerk.
